result.summary: Pausanias surveys the great benefactors of Greece from Miltiades to Philopoemen, declaring Philopoemen the last. He ends with the Tegean inscription praising Philopoemen as a general and liberator.

scenes.title: Greece's benefactors surveyed
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists Greek leaders from Miltiades to Aratus, judging who truly served all Greece rather than a single state.

scenes.title: Inscription for Philopœmen at Tegea
scenes.summary: Pausanias quotes the verses on Philopoemen's statue, praising his wisdom, cavalry command, victories over Spartan tyrants and defence of freedom.

notable_quotes.reason: Stark declaration that Greece no longer bred distinguished men.
Closing epitaph hailing Philopoemen as winner of his country's freedom.

analysis.text: Pausanias judges greatness by service to all Greece, mourning the decline of Greek independence after Philopoemen.
Writing under Roman rule, Pausanias treats Philopoemen's era, ended by Rome's conquest in 146 BC, as the close of Greek heroism.

language_notes.text: Codrus was a legendary Athenian king who died to save Athens; Aristomenes led the Messenians against Sparta. Their battles were for their own people.
Pausanias (son of Cleombrotus), the Spartan victor at Platæa, later plotted with Persia; this is the 'subsequent crimes'. He is not the author.
Decemvirates were ruling boards of ten men, set up in cities under Spartan influence; Epaminondas ended them.
Leosthenes led Greek forces in the Lamian War after Alexander's death; Pausanias refers to Aratus' earlier treatment in his Sicyon section.
'When slavery was growing' means when subjection to tyrants was spreading; Philopœmen checked it, as the verse claims.

context_notes.text: Miltiades commanded the Athenians at Marathon in 490 BC. Philopœmen of Megalopolis (died 183 BC) was called 'the last of the Greeks'.
Leonidas, king of Sparta, died holding Thermopylæ in 480 BC; Themistocles built the Athenian fleet and won at Salamis.
Messene (369 BC) and Megalopolis were founded with Epaminondas' help to check Spartan power.

literary_notes.text: The blunt, elegiac opening shows the author's judgment, framing the whole survey as a decline of Greek greatness.
Saying the war's famous victors almost ruined Greece with their own hands exaggerates to condemn civil strife.
'As wise in the council-chamber as brave in the field' balances civil and military excellence to praise Philopœmen.
